summaries.summary: MRC requires answering passage questions by predicting answer spans, with datasets including SQuAD, MS MARCO, and TriviaQA and models including BiDAF, R-NET, and QANet.
MRC models differ from human beings in data hunger and noise robustness because humans also use general knowledge, especially inter-word semantic connections.
Integrating MRC neural networks with human general knowledge requires extraction and utilization, with WordNet chosen for inter-word semantic connections and explicit utilization explored.
The paper proposes a WordNet-based data enrichment method and Knowledge Aided Reader (KAR), which is comparable to state-of-the-art models and more robust to noise.
This section elaborates a WordNet-based data enrichment method that controllably extracts inter-word semantic connections from each passage-question pair as general knowledge.
WordNet organizes words into synsets with sixteen semantic relation types, and semantic relation chains link synsets through concatenated relations with hops.
Inter-word semantic connections are determined using extended synsets, a maximum hop count hyper-parameter, and a heuristic rule based on shared extended synsets.
General knowledge extraction records positions of semantically connected passage words, with the hyper-parameter controlled by cross validation due to useless extracted results.
Knowledge Aided Reader (KAR) explicitly uses extracted general knowledge to assist its knowledge aided mutual attention and knowledge aided self attention mechanisms.
The task is to predict an answer span from a passage and relevant question so that the resulting passage subsequence answers the question.
KAR is an end-to-end MRC model consisting of five layers.
The Lexicon Embedding Layer maps words to lexicon embeddings using pre-trained GloVe word vectors, CNN character embeddings, and a shared dense layer with ReLU activation.
The Context Embedding Layer maps lexicon embeddings to context embeddings using a shared bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) and concatenating forward and backward outputs.
The Coarse Memory Layer uses knowledge aided mutual attention and a BiLSTM to produce coarse memories as question-aware passage representations.
The Refined Memory Layer uses knowledge aided self attention and a BiLSTM to produce refined memories as final passage representations.
The Answer Span Prediction Layer predicts the answer start position and answer end position based on the above layers.
Trainable parameters, refined memories, question summaries, and vector concatenation are used to obtain the answer end position distribution.
An answer span prediction matrix is constructed, with training minimizing a loss and inference taking row and column indices of its maximum element.
Knowledge aided mutual attention fuses question context embeddings into passage context embeddings by calculating similarities between passage and question context embeddings.
The existing similarity function is modified because introducing pre-extracted general knowledge into high-level context embedding similarities should make results more reasonable.
Enhanced context embeddings are constructed from pre-extracted general knowledge by gathering matching context embeddings and forming an attended matching vector.
Trainable parameters and a dense layer with ReLU activation are used to obtain the enhanced context embedding.
Knowledge aided mutual attention constructs a knowledge aided similarity matrix and passage-attended question summaries and question-attended passage summaries.
Softmax along row and column dimensions and a dense layer with ReLU activation produce the outputs of knowledge aided mutual attention.
Knowledge aided self attention fuses coarse memories using pre-extracted general knowledge to involve only a precise subset of other passage words.
Trainable parameters and a dense layer with ReLU activation produce the fusion result and outputs of knowledge aided self attention.
Other attention mechanisms include multi-round alignment and using mutual attention as a skip-connector to densely connect pairwise layers.
Properly augmenting training examples can improve MRC model performance, as shown by generated questions and back-and-forth translation paraphrasing.
Multi-step reasoning addresses difficult MRC tasks using dynamically determined reasoning steps or fixed steps with stochastic dropout to avoid step bias.
Linguistic embeddings can be incorporated into MRC input layers, including POS embeddings, NER embeddings, and structural embeddings based on parsing trees.
Recent MRC breakthroughs benefit from feature-based transfer learning and fine-tuning-based transfer learning using models pre-trained on large external corpora.
The MRC dataset is SQuAD 1.1, with AddSent and AddOneSent adversarial sets used to evaluate robustness to noise from misleading sentences.
Implementation uses spaCy 2.0.13, WordNet 3.0, NLTK 3.3, TensorFlow 1.11.0, Adam, Exact Match (EM), F1 score, dropout, and exponential moving average.
KAR is compared with five top-20 single SQuAD 1.1 MRC models on development, test, and adversarial sets, showing comparable performance and greater robustness to noise.
Increasing INLINEFORM0 from 0 to 5 raises general knowledge monotonically, while KAR performance peaks at INLINEFORM1 3, and ablations and one-epoch results support general knowledge effectiveness.
KAR is compared with BIBREF10's encoding-based use of Wikipedia and ConceptNet knowledge, whose best EM INLINEFORM0 and F1 INLINEFORM1 are much lower.
Training subsets from sampling 1, 2, 3, and 4 questions per passage contain INLINEFORM0, INLINEFORM1, INLINEFORM2, and INLINEFORM3 examples, where KAR outperforms SAN and QANet.
Experimental results show KAR comparable in performance with state-of-the-art MRC models and superior in hunger for data and robustness to noise.

KAR integrates WordNet-based inter-word semantic connections into an end-to-end MRC model, achieves comparable performance and superior data efficiency and robustness, with future plans for ConceptNet and Freebase.
This work is partially supported by a research donation from iFLYTEK Co., Ltd., Hefei, China, and a discovery grant from Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (NSERC) of Canada.
